title: Sanding and abrasives
summary: Sanding removes small irregularities and prepares wood for finishing. Selecting the right abrasive and progressing from coarse to fine grit determine surface quality.
points: Purpose of sanding
Sanding removes small particles and machining marks, leaving a smooth surface ready for finishing. It generally follows sawing, milling or planing. (p. 62)
Abrasive grains
Natural abrasives include quartz and garnet; manufactured grains are more common. Aluminium oxide (corundum) is used on wood, while silicon carbide also suits veneer and varnished surfaces. (p. 62)
Understanding grit grades
Lower numbers mean coarser abrasives. The textbook gives P60–90 for rough work, P100–180 for finer sanding and P220–400 for varnish and filler; this is a guide, not a universal specification. (p. 62)
Hand-sanding procedure

Begin with a suitable coarse grade and progress to finer grades. Make final strokes with the grain. On flat surfaces use a sanding block with a compliant backing; sanding sponges suit curves. The textbook also describes lightly wetting the wood, allowing it to dry and sanding the raised fibres. (pp. 63–64)
Backing materials and selection
Abrasive grains are bonded to paper or cloth. Belts, mesh and abrasive wool also exist. Progress through a sensible sequence of grades to remove marks left by previous grit. (pp. 62–64)
facts: Grain materials
Natural: quartz and garnet. Synthetic: aluminium oxide and silicon carbide.
Backing
Paper, cloth, belts; sponges, wool and mesh for special surfaces.
Grit size
Lower number = coarser. Examples: 60–90 coarse, 100–180 fine, 220–400 varnish and filler.
Hand sanding
Begin coarser, progress finer, finish with the grain and use a sanding block.
Raised grain
Wet, dry and lightly resand before finishing when appropriate.
red: UPDATED INFORMATION: Modern coated abrasives generally use FEPA/ISO P-grit designations. A P-number is not simply the number of sieve openings per square inch as the older textbook explanation suggests. Follow the abrasive manufacturer's specification.

title: Mechanical fasteners and fittings
summary: Woodworking joints may use metal, wood or plastic fasteners. Important criteria are strength, the ability to dismantle the joint, accurate pilot holes and suitability for the materials.
points: Dismantling and materials

Fasteners include metal nails, staples, screws and bolts, wooden dowels and tongues, and plastic brackets. Some joints can be repeatedly dismantled, whereas others are damaged when taken apart. A mechanical joint is not necessarily a reusable knock-down joint. (pp. 66–67)
Nails and staples

A nail has a head, shank and point; nails often secure cabinet backs or small strips. The textbook recommends a nail length at least 2.5 times the attached material's thickness and slightly blunting a point near an edge to reduce splitting. Staples can substitute for nails and are common in upholstery. (pp. 67–68)
Wood screws

A wood screw consists of head, shank and thread. Heads may be countersunk, raised countersunk or round. The book suggests pilot holes to about three-quarters of the length of larger screws; choose drill diameter for the screw core and wood species rather than applying a universal rule. Use a matching driver bit. (pp. 68–69)
Knock-down connectors and tools

A bolt with a threaded barrel nut or an eccentric cabinet connector allows assembly and disassembly. Hammers, pliers and screwdrivers are used. PH uses a basic cross recess, whereas PZ has additional small recesses and requires a matching bit. (pp. 70–72)
Dowels, tongues and biscuits

Fluted beech dowels are commonly 6, 8, 10, 12 or 16 mm in the book; flutes distribute glue. A tongue fits into matching grooves. Biscuit joinery uses oval inserts in slots cut by a biscuit joiner, improving alignment and glued contact area. (pp. 73–74)
Plastic connectors
Plastic corner brackets with covers and trapezoidal connectors perform specific assembly tasks, such as securing a tabletop to its apron. (p. 75)
facts: Metal fasteners
Nails, staples, wood screws, bolts and fittings.
Nails
Head, shank and point; textbook guideline length at least 2.5× attached thickness.
Wood screws
Countersunk, raised countersunk or round head, shank and thread; predrill appropriately.
PH versus PZ
Different cross-head recesses and bits; correct matching avoids damage.
Knock-down hardware
Barrel nuts with bolts and eccentric cam connectors.
Wooden elements
Fluted dowels, loose tongues and biscuits.
Biscuits
Flat inserts in routed slots for alignment and increased bonded area.
Plastic elements
Corner brackets, dowels and trapezoidal connectors.
red: UPDATED INFORMATION: The textbook's 'drill to shank diameter' and 'three-quarters of screw length' rules are not universally valid. Pilot-hole diameter and depth depend on the screw core, timber species, distance from an edge and manufacturer instructions.

title: Glued joints
summary: Adhesive joints are permanent. Glue may join two surfaces directly or reinforce tenons, mortises, dowels, fingers and tongues. Joint quality depends on contact surfaces, appropriate adhesive, pressure and curing.
points: Purpose of a glued joint

Adhesive joints are normally non-dismantlable. A butt joint may rely on glue alone; a mortise-and-tenon, finger joint, dowel, biscuit or tongue-and-groove joint often gains strength from glue. Accurate mating surfaces matter. (p. 77)
Adhesive types

The textbook lists PVAc dispersion adhesives, urea-formaldehyde (UF) and traditional animal glues. Choose an adhesive based on moisture exposure, material and the manufacturer's technical data. (p. 77)
Applying and clamping
Spread adhesive with a brush, applicator or sprayer. Clamp the parts until the bond has cured sufficiently; releasing pressure too soon can weaken or damage the joint. (p. 77)
Clamps and jigs
A clamp generally includes a bar, fixed jaw, sliding jaw and pressure screw. Various sizes and special corner or frame jigs maintain alignment and force during bonding. (pp. 77–79)
facts: Adhesives
PVAc dispersion, UF and traditional animal-based glues listed by the textbook.
Clamps
Fixed and moving jaws apply pressure throughout the required setting period.
Principles
Accurate fit, appropriate glue spread, uniform clamping force and sufficient curing.
Important conditions
Follow the adhesive data sheet for open time, minimum temperature and wood moisture.

title: Wide and lengthwise wood joints
summary: Edge and end joints increase the width or length of solid-wood components. Accurate preparation, correct grain arrangement, suitable glue and clamping help keep panels flat and stable.
points: Widening and lengthening
Edge joints put boards side by side to make a wider panel. Length joints join their ends to produce longer pieces, such as continuous strips or finger-jointed stock. (pp. 80–82)
Edge-glued panel
A solid-wood panel is made from narrower boards glued together edge to edge. Match moisture content, prepare the edges accurately and arrange the boards to reduce warping. (pp. 80–81)
Board arrangement

The book illustrates arranging heartwood and sapwood sides, marking board order and choosing pieces for consistent appearance and dimensional stability. Check for clean and straight mating edges before gluing. (p. 81)
Gluing sequence
Select and mark boards, machine to size, apply glue along the joining edges, clamp the panel while checking flatness, then allow curing and dress the surface. (pp. 80–81)
Length joints
End joining differs from edge gluing. Finger joints or other end joints extend stock and permit use of shorter pieces of wood. (p. 82)
facts: Edge joints
Butt edges, tongue-and-groove, loose tongues and similar widening connections.
Edge-glued panel
Flat panel assembled from glued solid-wood strips.
Board selection
Appropriate ring orientation, equal moisture and freedom from major defects.
Gluing
Straight edges, glue spread, clamping, flatness checks and curing.
Length joints
Joining the ends of components, often using finger joints or laps.

title: Frames and structural joints
summary: Frame and corner joints transfer loads between wooden members. Choose them for loading, stock thickness, appearance and accurate mating surfaces.
points: Frame construction
Frame joints join members at corners or intermediate points. The loading, wood thickness, appearance and precision of fit determine the chosen joint. (pp. 84–85)
Tenon and open bridle joint

A common frame corner joint has a tenon on one part and an open-ended slot on the other. Mark and scribe parts accurately before cutting; typical hand tools include a square, marking gauge, saw and chisel. (pp. 85–87)
Mortise-and-tenon joint

A tenon fits a closed recess, or mortise, made with a mortise or bench chisel. The fit should be snug but not split the wood. The book also describes reinforced tongue-and-mortise variants for highly loaded furniture, including chairs and tables. (pp. 87–91)
Dowels and half-lap joints
Dowel joints require accurately aligned drilled holes. A half-lap joint removes part of each member's thickness to produce a flush overlap, at a corner or an intersection. (pp. 91–93)
Multiple tenons and tongues
Multiple tenons distribute load across a wider joint and may be through-tenons secured by wedges. Loose or integral tongues join panels and corners according to their design. (pp. 94–97, 107)
Finger and dovetail joints

Through dovetails show at both faces. Half-blind dovetails are hidden at one visible face, often a drawer front; secret dovetails are hidden at both. Sloping dovetail sides mechanically resist withdrawal. Precise layout and careful chiselling are essential. (pp. 98–104)
Sliding dovetail

A sliding dovetail consists of a matching trapezoidal groove and tongue. It helps guide or restrain a wide panel; the textbook shows a groove depth of roughly one-third panel thickness and an angle of approximately 20°. Allow for natural wood movement where required. (pp. 104–106)
Checking precision

Select and mark parts → lay out → saw tenons and cut mortises or slots → test-fit dry → correct mating faces → glue, clamp and check squareness. Files and rasps are not suitable for producing accurate flat tenon shoulders. (pp. 86–87, 99–100)
facts: Frame joints
Bridle joint, mortise-and-tenon, reinforced tenon variants, dowelled joints and lap joints.
Mortise and tenon
A projecting tenon enters a mating mortise; fit and bonding govern strength.
Half-lap
Part of both member thicknesses is removed to make an overlap.
Dovetails
Through, half-blind and secret joints; strong drawer and cabinet corners.
Dovetail shape
Wedge-like sides resist pulling the joint apart.
Sliding dovetail
Matching trapezoidal groove and tongue that helps stabilize a wide joint.
Preparation
Measure, lay out, machine, dry-fit, adjust, glue and check right angles.

title: Preparing wood for manufacture
summary: Before manufacture, timber is conditioned to the required moisture content and sometimes softened temporarily to improve its workability. It must also be protected from water and biological deterioration.
points: Purpose of preparation
Wood needs the right moisture level for manufacture and sometimes temporary softening to allow forming or veneer cutting. Protection from water and biological attack is also important. (p. 110)
Plasticization

Steaming or boiling applies heat and moisture to soften wood for bending, peeling or slicing. It changes the mechanical behaviour of lignin in cell walls; the behaviour changes again as the wood cools and dries. (p. 110)
Why timber is dried

Fresh timber contains water. Drying changes its dimensions and may cause checking, warping or distortion. Free water and bound water are distinguished; the aim is an appropriate moisture level for the intended environment. (p. 111)
Air drying

Stack sawn timber with correctly spaced stickers on raised supports and protect it from direct rain. Air circulation dries the individual pieces, while suitable sticker placement reduces deformation. (pp. 111–115)
Measuring moisture

The gravimetric method compares mass before drying with oven-dry mass: moisture content = (wet mass − dry mass) / dry mass × 100%. Electrical resistance meters give rapid practical estimates. (pp. 113–114)
Kiln drying

Kilns control temperature, relative humidity and air movement. The schedule must suit the wood species, dimensions and starting moisture, or defects and inadequate drying may result. Store timber appropriately afterwards. (pp. 115–118)
Design-based wood protection

Prevent prolonged wetting: keep timber off the ground, provide overhangs, drainage and ventilation, and avoid trapping moisture behind cladding. The textbook illustrates keeping exterior cladding approximately 300 mm above ground level. (pp. 118–120)
Chemical protection and safety

Preservatives target particular biological agents and must be selected for the exposure class and applied according to the product instructions. Dusty woodworking premises also require fire precautions: dust and chips can burn or explode. (pp. 118–121)
facts: Plasticization
Temporary increase in wood flexibility through heat and moisture, e.g. steam or boiling.
Moisture
Free and bound water affect dimensions and mechanical properties.
Air drying
Ventilated stickered stacks protected from rain.
Kiln drying
Controlled temperature, humidity and air flow according to a drying schedule.
Measurement
Gravimetric oven-drying method and electrical moisture meters.
Protection
Design measures against moisture and chemical treatment selected for exposure.
Hazards
Fungi, mould, insects, fire and moisture; ventilation and good storage matter.

title: Sawmill production
summary: Sawmills cut logs into boards, planks, beams, battens and strips. Sawn timber is classified by section size, thickness, width and the condition of its edges.
points: Converting logs into lumber

Longitudinal sawing turns logs into boards, thick planks, beams, smaller squared timbers, battens and strips. The terminology depends on cross-section, thickness, width and edge treatment. (pp. 122–124)
Unedged and edged timber

Unedged boards retain some curved outer surface of the log. Edged timber has its sides cut square. The textbook distinguishes boards from thick planks mainly by thickness, and beams from smaller squared timber by cross-section. (pp. 122–123)
Cross-section categories

According to the textbook, squared timber has width less than twice its thickness; smaller squared timber is no more than 100 mm thick, while larger beams exceed 100 mm. Battens have a cross-sectional area roughly 10–25 cm² and small strips up to 10 cm². These are textbook classifications. (pp. 123–124)
Sawing methods

Gang sawing uses several blades at once, for example a frame saw. Individual cutting uses band or circular saws. Sawing patterns affect lumber sizes and how much usable wood is recovered from a log. (pp. 125–126)
After sawing
Sort sawn wood, stack on spacers, dry it and store it to minimise defects and quality loss. (pp. 122–127)
facts: Log / sawlog
Raw material for processing in a sawmill.
Unedged sawn timber
Boards and planks with remaining rounded log edges.
Edged sawn timber
Beams, squared stock and other pieces with squared edges.
Small sections
Battens and thin strips distinguished by cross-section and use.
Sawing
Gang sawing with multiple blades, or individual cuts using e.g. band saws.
Sorting and storage
Classification by dimension and quality, appropriate stacking and protection.

title: Veneer and plywood manufacture
summary: Veneer is a thin sheet of wood cut from a log. It is used for decorative faces, plywood and other laminated products; the wood figure depends on the direction of cutting.
points: What veneer is
A veneer is a thin wood sheet separated from a log, used for visible surfaces or as a layer in plywood. Grain figure depends on the orientation of cutting relative to growth rings. (pp. 128–129)
Three manufacturing methods

Saw-cut veneer is produced with a saw, sliced veneer with a knife from a prepared log section, and rotary-cut veneer by peeling a turning log. These methods differ in material recovery and grain pattern. (pp. 128–129)
Log plasticization
Heat and moisture soften the wood before slicing or peeling to reduce cutting resistance and cracks. The effect on lignin in the cell walls is important. (pp. 128–129)
Drying and matching veneers
Peeled or sliced veneer has increased moisture after preparation and must be dried and graded. Decorative leaves are matched by grain pattern and required panel size. (pp. 129–130)
Plywood

Veneer layers are coated with adhesive, stacked usually with adjacent grain directions crossing, then pressed together. Cross-graining improves dimensional stability compared with solid wood; properties depend on species, bonding and ply count. (pp. 130–131)
facts: Veneer processes
Sawing, slicing and rotary peeling, often preceded by softening the log.
Grain figure
Depends on how the veneer is cut relative to growth rings.
Veneer preparation
Drying, grading, matching to panels and bonding.
Plywood
Multiple glued veneer plies pressed together; alternating grain directions reduce movement.
Types
Classified by species, number of plies, construction and intended use.

title: Blockboard manufacture
summary: Blockboard has a core made from wooden strips, faced with veneer on both sides. The face layers and core arrangement determine its properties.
points: Blockboard construction
This panel has a core assembled from wooden laths, with veneers glued to both faces. The construction and arrangement of its core influence performance. (p. 132)
Unglued core
The textbook describes string-linked cores: individual strips are temporarily held side by side during production without edge-gluing each strip to its neighbour. (p. 132)
Glued core
The strips are edge-glued. They are made from prepared wood laths or other wood elements; manufacture must ensure even thickness and stability. (p. 133)
Manufacturing sequence
Make the strip core, apply adhesive and veneer layers to both sides, press the complete panel, then trim and finish it. (pp. 132–133)
facts: Construction
Solid-wood strip core plus veneer layers on both sides.
Core types
Strips joined by gluing or held together by another production method.
Core material
Solid wood strips or other suitable arrangements according to the product.
Applications
Furniture and interior panels where blockboard properties are appropriate.

title: Wood-based particle and fibre panels
summary: Engineered wood panels are made from chips, strands, fibres or sawdust combined with binders and pressed into sheets. Particle size, orientation, density and adhesive determine their behaviour.
points: Principle
Wood chips, strands, fibres or sawdust are mixed with a suitable binder and pressed into flat panels. Particle size, alignment, density and binder type control properties. (p. 134)
Particleboard (DTD)

Particleboard is pressed from wood particles and adhesive and can have finer particles on the faces and coarser particles in the core. It is widely used for furniture and as a substrate for surface finishes. The book also covers extrusion-pressed forms. (pp. 134–135)
OSB

Oriented strand board uses long slender wood strands aligned in layers, with the outer layers predominantly along the board length. The application depends on board grade, service conditions and direction of loading. (p. 136)
MFP
Multi-function panels are made from longer particles or strands but with an arrangement different from the strongly oriented layers of OSB. (p. 137)
Fibreboard

Wood is broken down into fibres. Different manufacturing methods and densities produce soft insulating panels, medium-density fibreboard (MDF) and harder high-density panels (HDF). MDF is formed from fibres mixed with binder and hot-pressed. (pp. 138–141)
Other boards and selection

The textbook also describes sawdust panels and cement-bonded particleboards. Select a product by loading, moisture exposure, machinability, appearance and finish. A general material group name does not establish suitability for damp conditions or structural loads. (pp. 142–143)
facts: Particleboard / DTD
Wood particles bonded with adhesive and pressed into boards.
OSB
Oriented strand board with aligned long strands, often for construction.
MFP
Multipurpose panels of longer particles with a different strand arrangement.
Fibreboard / MDF / HDF
Wood-fibre panels; MDF has medium density and HDF high density.
Other types
Sawdust panels, cement-bonded boards and other composites.
Selection criteria
Exposure, structural loads, machinability, surface finish and adhesive emissions.
red: UPDATED INFORMATION: For wood-based boards, check the current product datasheet and classification for structural or damp environments. Historical nomenclature alone is not enough for specifying construction applications.
